Orientation: Stand before the majestic "Harpe by Naderman (Paris, 1780)" at the Palais Lascaris, and let your gaze travel along its elegant curve. From this vantage point, the intricate painted floral motifs adorning the soundboard come to life, revealing the artistry of an era.

The harp, crafted by Jean-Henri Naderman in Paris in 1780, carries with it the whispers of its former owner, the Viscountess of Beaumont. This exquisite instrument was hidden away in the attic of the Château de Busset in Allier, France, until the City of Nice purchased it in 2007, rescuing it from obscurity. In May 2008, it was unveiled to the public for the first time at the Palais Lascaris during the European Night of Museums, becoming a cherished part of the museum's renowned collection.

This harp, with its height of 161.5 cm, is a testament to the craftsmanship of the late 18th century. The wood and various materials used in its construction speak to the luxurious tastes of the time. Among its standout features is the single-action hook mechanism, a pedal-operated system that allowed musicians to change keys with ease, an innovation of its day. The soundboard, adorned with painted floral and vegetal motifs, culminates in a painted landscape scene framed by carved acanthus leaves at the base, offering a visual feast that complements its auditory purpose.

The Palais Lascaris, a 17th-century aristocratic building, underwent significant architectural changes in the 18th century, mirroring the evolution of the harp itself. The museum, with its focus on 17th- and 18th-century instruments, provides a fitting home for this harp. Its presence here not only enriches the historical narrative of the collection but also offers a glimpse into the cultural tapestry of its era.

As you stand before this harp, consider how the demands of English music and the subsequent innovations in harp design would shape future instruments, paving the way for the more complex double-action harps of the 19th century. This harp is a bridge between past and future, a silent witness to the evolution of musical artistry.

Orientation: Stand to the side of the Basse de violon by Paolo Antonio Testore (Milan, 1696) to appreciate its full body length and the craftsmanship that remains untouched by time.

The basse de violon, attributed to the Milanese luthier Carlo Giuseppe Testore, originally retained its oversized body format typical of the late 17th century. Unlike many similar instruments that were altered in the 18th and 19th centuries to match modern cello proportions, this one avoided such modifications. As a result, the instrument remains a rare example of its kind and entered the collection of the city of Nice through the bequest of Antoine Gautier in 1904, preserving its historical integrity for future generations.

This particular basse de violon stands as a testament to the artistic lineage of the Testore family, who carved a niche in the world of luthiery under the guidance of Carlo Giuseppe, a pupil of the renowned Giovanni Grancino. The Testores were known for their craftsmanship, and this instrument is a shining example of their expertise, echoing the rich sounds of an era when the violone was a staple in orchestras and ensembles.

The bass viol itself is a remarkable piece of craftsmanship. The wood, likely aged spruce or maple, has a warmth and resonance that speaks to centuries of musical tradition. Its oversized body is a visual reminder of its historical roots, predating the modern cello. This viol is a living relic, its unaltered form a window into a time when music and instrument-making were both art and science. The intricate scrollwork and careful varnishing add to its allure, reflecting the dedication of its maker to both function and beauty.

Housed within the Palais Lascaris, a seventeenth-century aristocratic building once owned by the Vintimille-Lascaris family, the viol is part of a broader collection showcasing the evolution of musical instruments. This setting enriches its narrative, as the palace itself has transitioned from a noble residence to a museum dedicated to preserving the sounds of the past. As you reflect on this instrument, consider the lasting impact of these historical pieces on modern music, reminding us of the delicate balance between tradition and innovation.

The best view is from slightly to the side, where the gleam of its brass and the intricacy of its U-shaped slide, with two parallel sliding tubes, become most apparent.

In 1901, the city of Nice was graced with a generous bequest from Antoine Gautier, a passionate music collector. Among the treasures was the Sacqueboute ténor crafted by Anton Schnitzer in Nuremberg in 1581. This instrument is particularly noteworthy for retaining its original slide and acoustic components, setting it apart as one of the earliest surviving sackbuts in such pristine condition. Thanks to Gautier's foresight, this rare piece found its way to the Palais Lascaris in 2001, where it now resides as a key part of the museum's collection.

This tenor sackbut, known in old French as a saqueboute, is a type of trombone. It stands as the oldest preserved example of its kind in the world, still in its original state. The bell rim bears the inscription 'MACHT ANTONI SCHNITZER A[NNO] MDLXXXI,' a testament to Schnitzer's meticulous craftsmanship. His mark is shared with another instrument from the same period, linking them through time and skill. The brass mouthpiece, surviving alongside the main body, offers a rare glimpse into the instrument-making practices of the late Renaissance.

The instrument's U-shaped slide is a distinctive feature, allowing for the smooth movement necessary to achieve varied pitches and tones. This design was revolutionary for the time, enabling musicians to explore new musical expressions. As you recall the Violes gambe by William Turner from earlier in your tour, consider the connection between string and brass innovations in shaping the soundscapes of their eras.

This sackbut, with its blend of historical significance and technical ingenuity, speaks to a time when musical boundaries were being expanded. It stands quietly within the ornate walls of the Palais Lascaris, a silent witness to the evolution of music. Next, let’s explore how the French Revolution influenced the design of the harp you first encountered.

Orientation: Stand at the center of the salon and let your gaze settle on the bass viola da gamba by William Turner from 1652. From this vantage, the instrument's subtle craftsmanship and historical aura become fully palpable, inviting a deeper look into its storied existence.

In 1901, Antoine Gautier, an amateur musician and avid collector, bequeathed his collection of musical instruments to the city of Nice. This significant donation included the rare 1652 bass viola da gamba crafted by the English luthier William Turner. As a result of Gautier's bequest, the viol eventually found a permanent home at the Palais Lascaris in the 2000s, where it is preserved in playable condition and used for live concerts, ensuring its continued musical legacy.

This bass viola da gamba, adorned with six strings, is a testament to Turner's mastery of his craft during the tumultuous Commonwealth period. The instrument bears Turner's signature heart-shaped carved rosette beneath the fingerboard, a detail that speaks to the intricate artistry of its maker. Such viols were rare survivors of their time, as many were altered or dismantled to meet the changing musical tastes of later centuries. This viol's existence is a rare glimpse into the past, offering a living soundscape of 17th-century England.

The viol's creation in Gravel Lane near Aldgate, London, came at a time when musicians were adapting to the increased demand for intimate chamber music, a shift spurred by the English Civil War's disruptions. This historical context adds a layer of intrigue to what might seem like a mere string instrument, revealing its role in the evolving soundscape of its era.

As you reflect on the viol, consider the broader collection of the Palais Lascaris, where Italian craftsmanship, like that seen in the bass violin by Paolo Antonio Testore, complements Turner's English tradition. What innovations did these Italian craftsmen bring to the world of bass instruments? This question lingers, inviting you to explore further.

Orientation: As you stand before the Sacqueboute ténor by Anton Schnitzer, observe its elegant form and the intricate craftsmanship that has survived over four centuries. From this vantage point, you can truly appreciate the mastery involved in creating such an enduring instrument.

The story of this remarkable instrument begins in 1901 when Antoine Gautier, a devoted music enthusiast, bequeathed his collection to the city of Nice. Among these treasures was the Sacqueboute ténor, crafted by Anton Schnitzer in Nuremberg in 1581. This instrument is noteworthy for retaining its original U-shaped slide and acoustic components, a rare feat among Renaissance sackbuts. In 2001, thanks to Gautier's gift, the instrument found its permanent home in the Palais Lascaris, a testament to his dedication to preserving musical history.

Schnitzer, active in the mid-16th century, was renowned for his expertise in brass instrument-making. His mark, engraved on the bell garland, remains a signature of his craft. Before its residency at the Palais Lascaris, the Sacqueboute was part of the Conservatoire National de Région de Nice's collection, underscoring its historical importance. This sackbut is one of only thirteen surviving Renaissance models worldwide, making it a centerpiece of the museum's collection. The presence of its original brass mouthpiece is an exceptionally rare survival, further enhancing its value. As you continue through the Palais Lascaris, consider how pieces like this tenor sackbut connect with others you've seen, like the violes gambe by William Turner, offering a rich tapestry of musical evolution.

Orientation: Stand close to the harp, allowing you to fully appreciate the intricate floral and vegetal motifs painted on the soundboard, which culminate in an exquisite landscape scene at the base, framed by carved acanthus leaves.

The harp, crafted by Jean-Henri Naderman in Paris in 1780, once graced the halls of the Viscountess of Beaumont's residence. After her time, this magnificent instrument was stowed away in the attic of the Château de Busset in Allier, France, where it quietly rested until rediscovered. In 2007, the City of Nice purchased this historical gem, rescuing it from obscurity. As a result, it was first publicly presented at the Palais Lascaris during the European Night of Museums in May 2008, becoming a celebrated part of the museum's collection.

The harp stands at 161.5 cm and features a single-action hook mechanism controlled by pedals, a testament to Naderman's innovative craftsmanship of the late 18th century. The soundboard's decoration is not merely ornamental; it represents the artistic sensibilities of the period, merging visual beauty with musical elegance. The painted floral and vegetal motifs lend a vivid imagination to the instrument, while the landscape scene framed by acanthus leaves at the base anchors it in a tradition of storytelling through art.

The Palais Lascaris itself is a fitting home for such an instrument, housed in a 17th-century building that underwent significant alterations in the 18th century, mirroring the harp's own journey through history. Part of a collection that transitioned to the Palais from the Musée Masséna in 2001, the harp contributes to a broader narrative of musical evolution from the 17th to the 20th century. The exhibition not only highlights individual instruments but also invites contemplation of the cultural and historical contexts in which they thrived.

Orientation: Stand close to the display of the Basse de violon by Paolo Antonio Testore, taking in the details of its oversized body. This vantage point allows you to appreciate the craftsmanship that has preserved its original 17th-century form, providing a unique contrast to the more modern pieces you've encountered.

The basse de violon, attributed to the Milanese luthier Carlo Giuseppe Testore, retains its oversized body format typical of the late 17th century. Unlike many similar instruments that were altered in the 18th and 19th centuries to match modern cello proportions, this one avoided such modifications. As a result, the instrument remains a rare example of its kind and entered the collection of the city of Nice through the bequest of Antoine Gautier in 1904, preserving its historical integrity for future generations.

Carlo Giuseppe Testore, inspired by his teacher Giovanni Grancino, founded his workshop in Milan, producing instruments renowned for their superior quality. This particular basse de violon showcases not just the craftsmanship but also the continuity of artistry passed down within the Testore family, influencing the evolution of stringed instrument making. In the 18th century, Testore's workshop became known for maintaining the tradition while adapting to the changing demands of musicians, ensuring that their creations remained relevant in an evolving musical landscape.

The instrument's journey to the Palais Lascaris is part of a larger narrative: Antoine Gautier's passion for music led him to assemble a collection that would become a cornerstone of the museum's holdings. His dedication ensured that rare instruments like this basse de violon would be accessible to the public, enriching the cultural fabric of Nice. Standing before it, you witness a piece of history that bridges the past and present, its resonance still felt in the world of music today. This legacy not only celebrates the craftsmanship of the Testore family but also highlights the enduring influence of luthiers who shaped the course of musical expression.

Orientation: Stand back from the elegant display of Violes gambe by William Turner, crafted in 1652, to fully appreciate the carefully preserved details that emerge when viewed as a whole.

In 1901, Antoine Gautier, an amateur musician and avid collector, bequeathed his collection of musical instruments to the city of Nice. This significant donation included the rare 1652 bass viola da gamba crafted by English luthier William Turner. The viol, noted for its six strings and Turner's signature heart-shaped carved rosette below the fingerboard, eventually found a permanent home at the Palais Lascaris in the 2000s, where it is preserved in playable condition and used for live concerts, ensuring its continued musical legacy.

William Turner, who was active in London near Aldgate in the mid-17th century, crafted this instrument during the English Civil War period, a time when musicians were increasingly adapting to the demand for intimate chamber music. This bass viola da gamba stands as a rare testament to Turner's expertise, as many similar viols were dismantled or altered in later centuries to suit evolving musical tastes, often being transformed into cellos. The instrument's preservation and ongoing use in concerts at Palais Lascaris highlight its historical and cultural significance, connecting the past to the present through its continued voice in live performances. Here, amid the grandeur of this 17th-century aristocratic residence, echoes of Turner's craftsmanship reverberate, bridging time through music. As you reflect on its legacy, consider the innovations that Italian craftsmen would later bring to the world of bass instruments, forever altering the musical landscape.

Orientation: Stand back to appreciate the Sacqueboute ténor by Anton Schnitzer, crafted in Nuremberg in 1581. Its U-shaped slide and parallel tubes, a hallmark of early trombone design, remain intact, offering a glimpse into musical craftsmanship from over four centuries ago.

In 1901, the city of Nice received a significant bequest from Antoine Gautier, an avid music lover and collector, who assembled an outstanding collection of musical instruments. This collection included the remarkable Sacqueboute ténor made by Anton Schnitzer, which is distinguished by its original slide and acoustic components. Because of Gautier's donation, this rare instrument was transferred to the municipal collection and eventually found a home in the Palais Lascaris in 2001, where it continues to be preserved as part of the museum's collection.

Anton Schnitzer, renowned for his expertise in brass instrument-making, produced this tenor sackbut, which remains one of the thirteen surviving examples of Renaissance sackbuts globally. The instrument bears Schnitzer's mark, along with the engraved date '1581' on its bell garland, linking it to his family's pivotal role in the world of brass-making in Nuremberg. Despite the passage of time, the piece retains its original matching brass mouthpiece, an exceptionally rare feature for 16th-century brass instruments.

As you stand before this instrument, note how its historical and acoustic integrity have been preserved. This sackbut's inclusion in the Palais Lascaris underscores the museum's dedication to preserving musical heritage, connecting it to the broader collection that includes the violes gambe by William Turner you've already seen. The tenor sackbut stands not only as a testament to Anton Schnitzer's craftsmanship but also as a bridge to the past, highlighting the evolution of music and instrument-making through the ages.

Orientation: Stand back a few steps from the Harpe by Naderman (Paris, 1780) to appreciate its full height of 161.5 centimeters and the intricate floral motifs painted along its soundboard. This vantage point reveals the delicate craftsmanship of Jean-Henri Naderman and the graceful silhouette that echoed through the aristocratic homes of the late 18th century.

The harp, crafted by Jean-Henri Naderman in Paris in 1780, once belonged to the Viscountess of Beaumont. After serving as a centerpiece in her residence, this exquisite instrument was hidden away in the attic of the Château de Busset in Allier, France. In 2007, the City of Nice purchased this historical instrument, rescuing it from obscurity. This acquisition was part of an effort to enrich the city's cultural offerings, in line with the historical musical instrument collections transferred to the Palais Lascaris from the Musée Masséna in 2001. The harp was first presented publicly at the Palais Lascaris during the European Night of Museums in May 2008, where it became a part of the museum's esteemed collection.

This harp operates on a single-action hook mechanism, controlled by pedals, allowing musicians to alter the pitch of the strings. Such a mechanism was an engineering achievement of its time, providing performers with greater flexibility in their repertoire. The decorative elements, including acanthus leaves that frame a painted landscape scene at the base, speak to the artistic elegance and technical skill of Naderman, whose name is engraved on the internal maker's label. 

The Palais Lascaris itself, a seventeenth-century aristocratic building, underwent significant architectural changes in the eighteenth century, mirroring the innovative spirit of the ages. As you stand before the harp, consider how such instruments influenced musical compositions and performances of their era, laying the groundwork for future developments in harp design and functionality.

Orientation: Stand close to the bass viol by Paolo Antonio Testore, examining the robust and oversized body that defies modernization. From here, its craftsmanship as a preserved 17th-century piece becomes unmistakably clear.

The basse de violon, attributed to the Milanese luthier Carlo Giuseppe Testore, retains its oversized body format typical of the late 17th century. Unlike many similar instruments that were altered in the 18th and 19th centuries to match modern cello proportions, this one avoided such modifications. Testore, having learned his craft under the guidance of Giovanni Grancino, founded his workshop in Milan where he and later his sons continued to produce instruments renowned for their robust sound and elegant lines. As a result, the instrument remains a rare example of its kind and entered the collection of the city of Nice through the bequest of Antoine Gautier in 1904, preserving its historical integrity for future generations. Gautier, an avid collector, ensured that such treasures would find a resting place in Nice, enriching the city's cultural landscape.

The architectural backdrop of the Palais Lascaris, once a residence of the Vintimille-Lascaris family until 1802, provides historical context to the rich heritage of these instruments. This particular basse de violon not only showcases the craftsmanship of the Testore family but also underscores the preservation of musical traditions across centuries. With its thickly varnished surface and the distinct curves of its body, it visually echoes the opulent surroundings of a palace turned museum. As you reflect on this piece within the broader collection, its place in the evolution of string instruments becomes not just evident but celebrated. The transformation of the Palais Lascaris into a museum of musical instruments further cements the legacy left by creators like Testore, who shaped the sounds that still resonate today.

Orientation: Stand facing the display where the bass viola da gamba is housed, allowing your eyes to trace the intricate rosette beneath the fingerboard—an emblem of William Turner's craftsmanship, visible only from this angle.

In 1901, the esteemed collector and amateur musician Antoine Gautier profoundly impacted the cultural tapestry of Nice. He bequeathed his remarkable collection of musical instruments to the city, which included the 1652 bass viola da gamba crafted by the renowned English luthier William Turner. This donation was officially accepted in 1904, leading to its eventual home in the Palais Lascaris during the 2000s. Turner's instrument, remarkable for its six strings, survived a period when many viols succumbed to alterations or destruction. Created during the English Commonwealth period, many similar instruments were transformed into cellos to adapt to evolving musical preferences. Yet, Turner's viol endures, with its delicately carved heart-shaped rosette intact, serving as both historical artifact and working instrument. It echoes through the hallowed salon of the Palais, harking back to a time when intimate chamber music flourished against the backdrop of civil unrest.

Turner, actively crafting instruments in London near Aldgate between 1647 and 1656, demonstrated extraordinary resilience amid the turbulent backdrop of the English Civil War. By employing exquisite craftsmanship and a distinctive design, he ensured that his viols would not only serve their era but would also become cherished relics for generations. Today, the viola da gamba stands as a testament to a time when music adapted to the intimate settings necessitated by the era's socio-political upheaval, much like the sacqueboute ténor by Anton Schnitzer you stopped at earlier. As you stand here, consider the innovations Italian craftsmen brought to bass instruments, a future that Turner's creation hints at, sitting quietly among the remarkable collection of the Palais Lascaris.

Orientation: Stand a few steps back from the Harpe by Naderman (Paris, 1780) and observe its elegant silhouette. From this angle, the intricate floral and vegetal motifs painted on the soundboard reveal themselves, a testament to the artisanal craftsmanship of its era.

The Harpe by Naderman, crafted by Jean-Henri Naderman in Paris in 1780, carries a narrative as rich as its decoration. This harp once belonged to the Viscountess of Beaumont, a significant patron, and collector in her time, who cherished this instrument as a centerpiece in her residence. Her possession of the harp signifies the cultural and social importance of music in aristocratic circles of the period. When her era came to an end, the harp was tucked away in the attic of the Château de Busset in Allier, France. It was Jean-François, a descendant of Naderman's lineage, who later rediscovered the instrument. Recognizing its historical value and exquisite craftsmanship, the City of Nice acquired it in 2007. Jean-François' discovery rescued the harp from obscurity, setting the stage for the City of Nice, under the guidance of its cultural leaders, to present it publicly at the Palais Lascaris for the European Night of Museums in May 2008. This careful restoration and presentation reflected the ongoing efforts to enrich Nice's cultural heritage.

The harp itself stands at 161.5 cm and features a single-action hook mechanism controlled by pedals. This design choice, characteristic of the late 18th century, allowed musicians to change pitch easily, offering more expressive possibilities in performances. The painted landscape scene at the base, framed by acanthus leaves, invites viewers to reflect on the intersection between visual and musical artistry. Now part of the esteemed collection of historical musical instruments at Palais Lascaris, this harp not only exemplifies the craftsmanship of its time but also serves as a bridge connecting the past with contemporary appreciation. The preservation and display of such instruments underscore the city's dedication to celebrating the multifaceted nature of art, music, and history.

Orientation: Stand before the bass viola da gamba crafted by William Turner in London, 1652. From this vantage point, the intricate heart-shaped carved rosette below the fingerboard, a hallmark of Turner's craftsmanship, becomes pronounced against the dark wood, inviting contemplation of its rich history.

In 1901, Antoine Gautier, an amateur musician and fervent collector, bequeathed his invaluable collection of musical instruments to the city of Nice. Within this collection lay a rare gem: the 1652 bass viola da gamba, crafted by the skilled English luthier William Turner. Known for his work in Gravel Lane near Aldgate, Turner fashioned this instrument during the mid-17th century, a time when the English Civil War gave rise to an increased appreciation for chamber music and intimate gatherings. His viola's characteristic heart-shaped carved rosette, a signature element, reflects Turner's meticulous attention to detail, which ensured not only the instrument's aesthetic beauty but also its enduring sonority.

Officially accepted by the city in 1904, Gautier's donation eventually found its rightful home at the Palais Lascaris in the 2000s. The viol remains a testament to Turner's expertise during an era when many such instruments were either dismantled or altered to accommodate changing musical trends. Amidst the salon's grandeur, what distinguishes Turner's creation is its tangible legacy; it is maintained in playable condition and frequently used for concerts, allowing contemporary audiences to experience its historical resonance.

Unlike the sackbut, which you paused at earlier, Turner's viola da gamba endures as a bridge between past and present, offering a rare auditory experience. As you ponder this instrument's journey from a bustling 17th-century London workshop to the opulent halls of the Palais Lascaris, consider what the Italian craftsmen brought to bass instruments. Their innovations beckon, hinting at new levels of craftsmanship and sound quality that awaited viols like this one.

Orientation: Position yourself to admire the bass viol by Paolo Antonio Testore, attributed to 1696, and you’ll witness the grandeur of Milanese craftsmanship not diminished by time or alteration. This instrument's large body, surviving untouched by centuries of changing musical tastes, dominates the space, echoing the story of its preservation.

The basse de violon, attributed to the Milanese luthier Carlo Giuseppe Testore, retains its oversized body format typical of its late 17th-century origin. Testore, a pupil of renowned luthier Giovanni Grancino, founded his workshop in Milan, where he and his sons crafted instruments that defied the passage of time. Unlike many similar instruments, altered in the 18th and 19th centuries to match modern cello proportions, this particular viol remains a rare example of the original bass violin design. It entered the collection of the city of Nice thanks to the bequest of Antoine Gautier in 1904, preserving its historical integrity for future generations.

Gautier, an amateur musician and fervent collector, actively contributed to preserving the musical heritage that now enriches this storied Palais. His passion for music meant that treasures like the basse de violon found a home in Nice, ultimately making their way to the Palais Lascaris. The testore family’s instruments, known for their craftsmanship, echo the dedication of their creators to both tradition and innovation. Here, in the Palais' 17th-century walls, once the residence of the Vintimille-Lascaris family, the viol stands not just as a testament to Milanese craftsmanship but also to a lineage that survived and thrived through turbulent times.

As you connect this piece to others you've encountered today—the harp from Paris, the viols of London—you'll notice this collection's narrative unfolds like a conversation across centuries. The grand architecture and intricate music weave together, carrying the spirit of craftsmanship and history. This continuity sets the stage for understanding how such instruments continue to influence modern music, inspiring awe and creativity in today’s musicians and audiences.

Orientation: Stand to the side of the Harpe by Naderman (Paris, 1780) in the display at Palais Lascaris, where the light catches its gilded elements and accentuates the intricate floral motifs on its soundboard.

The Harpe by Naderman, crafted in 1780 by Jean-Henri Naderman, a renowned harp maker in Paris, stands as a remarkable piece of musical history. At one point, this exquisite instrument found its home with the Viscountess of Beaumont, where it was treasured for its aesthetic and sonic beauty. Jean-Henri Naderman, known for his precision and artistry, produced this harp during an era when French culture thrived on elaborate musical compositions and performances, especially among the aristocracy. 

The harp embodies the elegance and craftsmanship of its time, with a single-action hook mechanism that was innovative for allowing harpists to change keys mid-performance. This capability revolutionized how harp music could be composed and played, enhancing the complexity and emotional depth of performances. Following its time with the Viscountess, the harp was stored in the Château de Busset in Allier, France, a shelter for many valuable artifacts of the time.

In 2007, the City of Nice purchased this historical instrument, rescuing it from obscurity to display it for public appreciation. It was first unveiled publicly at the Palais Lascaris during the European Night of Museums in May 2008. The purchase was part of a broader initiative to enrich the city’s cultural offerings and preserve historical musical instruments. Today, the harp stands as a testament to the rich cultural heritage that Naderman and his contemporaries infused into their craft, connecting visitors to the opulent soundscapes of 18th-century France. It continues to intrigue historians and music lovers alike, signifying a period when music was not just an art form but a crucial element of societal and cultural expression.

Orientation: Position yourself in front of the bass viola da gamba by William Turner, crafted in London in 1652. Notice the heart-shaped carved rosette beneath the fingerboard—a hallmark of Turner's craftsmanship. From here, you can appreciate the delicate woodwork and the historical weight this instrument carries.

In 1901, Antoine Gautier, an ardent collector and amateur musician, bequeathed his prized collection of musical instruments to the city of Nice. Among these treasures was the rare 1652 bass viola da gamba, crafted by the English luthier William Turner. His devotion to craft during the tumultuous times of the English Civil War period ensured this viol stood apart, even as many contemporaneous instruments were dismantled or altered in later years. The viol was officially accepted into Nice's public collections in 1904 and, in the 2000s, found its home at the Palais Lascaris. Here it continues to resonate within the walls of the salon during live performances, bridging centuries of musical tradition.

Turner, who worked in Gravel Lane near Aldgate, London, fashioned this instrument with six strings, a feature highlighting the demand for chamber music's intimate sounds during his time. Its survival, complete with the signature rosette, offers a tangible connection to the cultural shifts that swept through 17th-century England. This preserved history aligns with the broader collection at the Palais Lascaris, which features other period pieces like the sackbut you stopped at not long ago. Each contributes to a rich tapestry of sound that defined an era.

As you ponder Turner's viol, consider how Italian craftsmen later revolutionized the design of bass instruments after the viol's English heyday. What innovations did they bring that allowed the viola da gamba's legacy to evolve even further? Here, the past and the future of music intermingle, inviting endless exploration.

response_text: The Palais Lascaris in Nice, originally a 17th-century aristocratic residence, was purchased by the city in 1942 with the intent to transform it into a museum. This decision led to its classification as a historical monument in 1946, preserving its architectural heritage. Today, it stands as a musical instrument museum, housing the Violes gambe by William Turner, a rare 17th-century English bass viola da gamba. This instrument, part of the Gautier collection, was previously held across various Nice municipal institutions before finding a permanent home at the Palais Lascaris in the 2000s. Its presence here allows it to be maintained in playable condition, adding a living historical dimension to the museum's collection.

Orientation: As you stand here, let your gaze settle on the Sacqueboute ténor by Anton Schnitzer, crafted in 1581 in Nuremberg. This remarkable piece demands your attention, as it stands proudly on display, revealing its intricate U-shaped slide—a hallmark of the early trombone design.

The story of this sackbut begins humbly at the Conservatoire National de Région de Nice, where it was cherished for its historical value. In 2001, a pivotal moment occurred when this rare instrument found a new home at the Palais Lascaris. This move not only bestowed upon it a fitting backdrop of a seventeenth-century aristocratic palace but also allowed it to shine within the context of a grand music collection. The transition underscored the instrument's significance, enhancing the palace's reputation as a prominent musical museum in Nice.

Crafted by Anton Schnitzer the Elder, one of the renowned figures in brass instrument-making, this sackbut is among only thirteen surviving Renaissance sackbuts worldwide. Its glory lies not only in its age but in its original condition, maintaining the authentic slide and acoustic components that have remained untouched by modern alterations. The engraved inscription 'MACHT ANTONI SCHNITZER A[NNO] MDLXXXI' on its bell garland stands as an enduring testament to its creator's craftsmanship. This sackbut, the oldest preserved in its original state, becomes a bridge to the past, allowing us a glimpse into the musical world of the Renaissance.

The instrument's journey to Palais Lascaris also highlights the dedication to preserving musical heritage, aligning with other significant pieces in the collection, like the violes gambe by William Turner that you encountered earlier. Its presence here is a celebration of the rich tapestry of music history, offering a tangible connection to the sounds and stories of centuries past. As you ponder this, consider the next chapter in this journey: how the French Revolution's upheaval influenced the design and function of musical instruments, including the harp you admired in the first room.

Orientation: As you stand before the Harpe by Naderman (Paris, 1780), let your gaze travel from the ornate acanthus leaves at the base to the painted floral motifs flanking the strings. This perspective reveals the meticulous craftsmanship that defines this historical instrument.

In 1942, the city of Nice purchased the Palais Lascaris, setting the stage for its transformation from an aristocratic residence into a museum. The restoration began in 1962, turning the space into a haven for popular art and musical instruments. It was within this newly conceived museum that the Harpe by Naderman found its home after being unearthed from the attic of the Château de Busset. Acquired by the city of Nice in 2007, it was first revealed to the public during the European Night of Museums in May 2008.

Built in 1780 by Jean-Henri Naderman, the harp once belonged to the Viscountess of Beaumont, adding layers of aristocratic history to its provenance. The harp's soundboard is adorned with painted floral and vegetal motifs, culminating in a delicate landscape scene. This decorative choice echoes the Rococo style popular in the late 18th century, a period when music and art were deeply intertwined in French aristocratic life.

The harp employs a single-action hook mechanism, a system allowing musicians to alter the pitch of strings with foot pedals. This technical feature, although later surpassed by double-action mechanisms, was a significant advancement for its time, enabling more dynamic musical compositions.

The Palais Lascaris itself has undergone substantial architectural evolution, with significant alterations in the 18th century that reflect changes in taste and style. The building’s transformation into a museum in the mid-20th century underscores its resilience and adaptability.

The Harpe by Naderman is not just an instrument; it is a testament to the rich tapestry of French musical history, connecting the past's aristocratic salons to the present-day museum space, ensuring the legacy of its craftsmanship endures.

Orientation: Stand close to the glass case where Violes gambe by William Turner (Londres, 1652) is displayed. From this vantage point, you can appreciate the intricate craftsmanship of the bass viola da gamba, particularly the heart-shaped carved rosette below the fingerboard, a hallmark of Turner's work.

The Palais Lascaris in Nice, a former 17th-century aristocratic residence, was purchased by the city in 1942 with the aim of transforming it into a museum. This decision led to its classification as a historical monument in 1946, preserving its architectural heritage. Today, it stands as a musical instrument museum, housing the Violes gambe by William Turner, a rare 17th-century English bass viola da gamba. This instrument, part of the Gautier collection, was previously held across various Nice municipal institutions before finding a permanent home at the Palais Lascaris in the 2000s. Its presence here allows it to be maintained in playable condition, adding a living historical dimension to the museum's collection.

The bass viola da gamba was made in 1652 by the English luthier William Turner, who was active in London during the mid-17th century. This period, marked by the tumult of the English Civil War, was one where musical tastes shifted towards more intimate chamber music settings. The viol, with its six strings, is a testament to this era, offering a rich depth of sound suitable for the evolving musical landscape. The heart-shaped rosette below the fingerboard is not just an ornamental feature but a signature of Turner's craftsmanship, indicating the artist's attention to detail and dedication to his craft.

This instrument's survival is remarkable, especially considering that many similar viols from the Commonwealth period were dismantled or altered into cellos over the centuries. Its continued use in live concerts within the palace's salon brings the past to life, connecting us to the era's cultural and musical transitions. As you reflect on this piece, consider how it stands alongside other artifacts in this museum, like the sackbut you encountered earlier, which collectively illustrate the evolution of musical instruments through time.

The basse de violon attributed to Paolo Antonio Testore, dated to 1696, presents a curious anomaly because Paolo Antonio Testore was born around 1700. This discrepancy led experts to alternatively attribute the instrument to his father, Carlo Giuseppe Testore, who was active during the late 17th century. This unique characteristic has made it a significant piece within the Palais Lascaris collection, providing insight into the evolution of string instruments.

Orientation: Stand before the basse de violon by Paolo Antonio Testore, dated 1696, and let your eyes trace its robust, oversized body—a hallmark of its era and a tangible marker of its historical significance.

The basse de violon attributed to Paolo Antonio Testore, dated to 1696, presents a curious anomaly because Paolo Antonio Testore was born around 1700. This discrepancy led experts to alternatively attribute the instrument to his father, Carlo Giuseppe Testore, who was active during the late 17th century. As a result, this instrument has become a rare link to a time when bass violins were not yet modified to the modern cello proportions, retaining its original oversized body format. This unique characteristic has made it a significant piece within the Palais Lascaris collection, providing insight into the evolution of string instruments.

Crafted from fine woods, its warm, amber-hued varnish glimmers under the museum lights, revealing the meticulous craftsmanship that Testore's workshop was renowned for. Such attention to detail not only speaks to the artistic capabilities of the era but also to the Testore family’s legacy in advancing the art of violin making. The instrument's body, large and resonant, was designed to produce deep, sonorous tones—tones that once filled concert halls and salons with rich harmonies.

The Testore workshop, founded by Carlo Giuseppe Testore in Milan, was a hub of innovation and tradition. Carlo Giuseppe, a student of the esteemed Giovanni Grancino, imbued his instruments with both technical precision and aesthetic grace. This viol stands as a testament to that legacy, bridging the gap between the past and the present. It offers a window into the world of Baroque music, where such instruments were central to the era's orchestral and chamber music performances.

In the broader context of the Palais Lascaris, this basse de violon connects seamlessly with other historic instruments, like the violas da gamba you've already seen. Together, they form a narrative of musical evolution, illustrating how these early instruments laid the groundwork for those that would follow. The lasting impact of these creations on modern music is evident, as they continue to inspire and inform contemporary luthiers and musicians alike.

Orientation: Stand before the Harpe by Naderman (Paris, 1780) at Palais Lascaris and let your gaze travel from the intricate floral motifs on the soundboard to the carved acanthus leaves at the base, which frame a painted landscape scene. This perspective reveals the elegance of the 18th-century craftsmanship that embodies the historical richness of this instrument.

In 1942, the city of Nice purchased the Palais Lascaris with the intention of transforming it into a museum. This decision set in motion a series of restorations that began in 1962, reshaping the palace from a former aristocratic residence into a museum of popular art and musical instruments. As a result, the Harpe by Naderman, discovered in the attic of the Château de Busset and purchased by the city of Nice in 2007, found its home at the Palais Lascaris. It was first presented to the public during the European Night of Museums in May 2008.

Jean-Henri Naderman, a revered harp maker in Paris, crafted this particular harp in 1780. His work was renowned for its elegance and precision, serving the musical demands of the aristocracy, including the Viscountess of Beaumont, to whom this harp originally belonged. The harp's intricate design, featuring a single-action hook mechanism, reflects not only Naderman’s exceptional skill but also the cultural prestige it once held. 

Each element of the harp, from its wood to the delicate painted motifs, speaks to the opulence of its era. The design choices are not merely decorative but serve to enhance the instrument's acoustic qualities. The Palais Lascaris itself, altered significantly in the 18th century, provides a fitting backdrop for this harp, further contextualizing its historical significance. Thus, the harp does not merely stand as an isolated piece; it is a testament to the palace's ongoing celebration of musical heritage. As you observe, consider how the demands of French musical society at the time influenced the evolution of instruments like this harp, shaping their form and function.

Orientation: As you approach the display of the Sacqueboute ténor by Anton Schnitzer, pause to appreciate the craftsmanship evident in its U-shaped slide and the brass mouthpiece, details best seen when you stand slightly to the left. This angle reveals the distinctive features that mark it as one of the earliest surviving sackbuts.

The story of this instrument is deeply woven into the history of the Palais Lascaris. Originally part of the Conservatoire National de Région de Nice, the sackbut was relocated to the Palais Lascaris in 2001. This move was more than just a change of scenery. It placed the instrument within the opulent surroundings of a seventeenth-century aristocratic palace, where it could be appreciated not only for its musical significance but also within its historical context. This transition underscored the instrument's importance and helped establish the Palais Lascaris as a key musical instrument museum.

Anton Schnitzer, the creator of this sackbut, was active during the late Renaissance period and crafted this piece in 1581 in Nuremberg, known for its exquisite brass instruments. Schnitzer's work, identifiable by the engraved mark on the bell rim, showcases the remarkable craftsmanship of the era. One of the key features of this instrument is its slide mechanism with two parallel sliding tubes, a characteristic element of early trombones. This preserved original slide and brass mouthpiece highlight Schnitzer's dedication to quality and have allowed the instrument to maintain its historical and acoustic integrity over the centuries.

The sackbut was included in the municipal collections of Nice, thanks to a bequest from the passionate collector Antoine Gautier, who played a pivotal role in preserving musical heritage in the region. Gautier's contributions were instrumental in enriching the collection at the Palais Lascaris, where the sackbut now resides as a testament to the rich history of Renaissance brass instruments. This dedication to preservation continues to attract visitors who appreciate not only the physical beauty of the instrument but also its rich historical narrative.

The bass viol attributed to Paolo Antonio Testore, dated to 1696, presents a curious enigma. Since Paolo was born around 1700 and began working in the 1720s, experts have alternatively attributed this instrument to his father, Carlo Giuseppe Testore. Carlo Giuseppe was an esteemed Milanese luthier who founded the Testore workshop after studying under Giovanni Grancino. This familial lineage of craftsmanship, marked by intricate knowledge and skill, is embodied in the oversized body format of this instrument, avoiding the alterations many bass violins underwent to conform to modern cello proportions. This distinctive preservation offers a rare glimpse into the early design and character of bass violins before they adapted to changing musical needs.

Adding to its fascinating history, the instrument was part of a significant collection bequeathed by the devoted collector Antoine Gautier. This collection, rich with historical musical instruments, was transferred to Palais Lascaris as part of a project to transform it into a music museum, where it became a centerpiece. The setting within the former aristocratic residence of the Vintimille-Lascaris family enriches its narrative, creating a dialogue between the past and the present. As you reflect on the craftsmanship of Testore, consider how this viol, along with others like the Turner viol you saw earlier, continues to inform the innovation of modern string instruments.

Orientation: Stand near the center of the room to appreciate the full profile of the Violes gambe by William Turner (Londres, 1652), capturing the intricate details like the carved rosette and the warm patina that speaks of its storied past.

The Palais Lascaris in Nice, originally a 17th-century aristocratic residence, was purchased by the city in 1942 with the intent to transform it into a museum. This decision led to its classification as a historical monument in 1946, preserving its architectural heritage. Today, it stands as a musical instrument museum, housing the Violes gambe by William Turner, a rare 17th-century English bass viola da gamba. This instrument, part of the Gautier collection, was previously held across various Nice municipal institutions before finding a permanent home at the Palais Lascaris in the 2000s. Its presence here allows it to be maintained in playable condition, adding a living historical dimension to the museum's collection.

In the mid-17th century, English luthier William Turner crafted this bass viola da gamba in London, during a time when the country was recovering from the disruptions of the English Civil War. Turner, known for his workshop on Gravel Lane near Aldgate, produced several viols that stood out for their distinctive heart-shaped carved rosettes, a hallmark of his work. These instruments were in demand as chamber music grew increasingly popular, requiring instruments that could produce intimate soundscapes for smaller audiences. 

The instrument entered the public collections of Nice thanks to a bequest by Antoine Gautier, an amateur musician and collector who passed away in 1904. Gautier's legacy ensured that historical pieces like Turner's viol could be appreciated by future generations. The bass viola da gamba is often played in concerts held in the palace's salon, allowing modern audiences to experience its rich, resonant tones as they were heard centuries ago. The collection also forms a dialogue with other period pieces, such as the sacqueboute you stopped at a moment ago, illustrating the evolving landscape of sound that defined an era. As you stand before Turner's viol, consider the innovations Italian craftsmen would later bring to bass instruments — a story that continues to unfold in the historical halls of this museum.

Orientation: As you stand before the Harpe by Naderman (Paris, 1780) in the ornate halls of the Palais Lascaris, notice the intricate painted floral and vegetal motifs on its soundboard, accentuated by the rich history of its journey from obscurity to display.

In 1942, the city of Nice purchased the Palais Lascaris with the intention of transforming it into a museum. This decision set in motion a series of restorations that began in 1962, reshaping the palace from a former aristocratic residence into a museum of popular art and musical instruments. As a result of this transformation, the Harpe by Naderman, discovered in the attic of the Château de Busset and purchased by the city of Nice in 2007, found its home at the Palais Lascaris, where it was first presented to the public during the European Night of Museums in May 2008.

Jean-Henri Naderman, a prominent harp maker in Paris, crafted this particular harp in 1780. His expertise in designing harps that met the musical demands of the aristocracy culminated in this piece, once owned by the Viscountess of Beaumont. The harp features a single-action hook mechanism controlled by pedals, an innovation of its time that allowed harpists to modulate pitch mid-performance. This particular mechanism became a vital component that enhanced the complexity of compositions that could be played on the harp.

Moreover, François Joseph Naderman, Jean-Henri's son, continued the family legacy by establishing the harp studio at the Paris Conservatory in 1825, long after the creation of this harp. This studio became a focal point for harp education and innovation, nurturing generations of musicians who would carry forward the rich heritage encapsulated by Jean-Henri Naderman's craftsmanship. Through these family contributions to harp-making and music education, the Naderman name carved out a significant place in the history of Western music. 

As you take in the elegant artistry of this harp, consider how its crafted beauty and innovative design reflect not only the talents of its maker but also the evolving landscape of music in eighteenth-century France.

Orientation: As you stand before the Sacqueboute ténor by Anton Schnitzer from 1581, take a moment to observe the elaborate craftsmanship visible from this angle, particularly the U-shaped slide with its parallel sliding tubes—a distinctive hallmark of early trombones.

This remarkable instrument has a journey as compelling as its physical presence. Anton Schnitzer, known for his work in Nuremberg, crafted this tenor sackbut in 1581, offering a glimpse into the early design and construction that set the standard for brass instruments of its time. The instrument bears Schnitzer's mark with the engraved inscription, 'MACHT ANTONI SCHNITZER A[NNO] MDLXXXI', providing a direct link to its creator. For many years, this sackbut was held by the Conservatoire National de Région de Nice. The collection, however, underwent a significant transformation in 2001 when the instrument was relocated to the Palais Lascaris. This move brought the rare Renaissance sackbut into a new context, allowing it to be appreciated within the historical setting of a seventeenth-century aristocratic palace.

The relocation underscored the instrument's historical importance and enriched the cultural tapestry of the Palais Lascaris. In its new setting, the sackbut joins the broader narrative of the museum's exquisite collection, alongside the violes gambe by William Turner that you viewed earlier. Each aspect of the sackbut, from its original matching brass mouthpiece to its 10-millimetre diameter entrance bore, reflects the high level of preservation that makes this instrument one of the earliest surviving sackbuts in original condition. This preservation offers a rare, tangible connection to the musical practices of the 16th century—an auditory bridge to a time long past. In this context, the sackbut stands not just as a solitary artifact but as part of the living history within the ornate halls of Palais Lascaris. Orientation: Stand before the bass viola da gamba by William Turner, crafted in London in 1652. From this vantage, you can discern the heart-shaped carved rosette beneath the fingerboard, a signature feature of Turner's work. It invites you to imagine its resonance within the opulent surroundings of the Palais Lascaris.

In the quiet elegance of this seventeenth-century palatial museum, the Violes gambe by William Turner represents an intriguing vestige of history. Purchased by the city of Nice in 1942, the Palais Lascaris was transformed into a museum and named a historical monument by 1946. Within its storied walls lies this bass viola da gamba—an English masterpiece from the year 1652, intricately fashioned by Turner, who operated near London's Aldgate. This particular instrument survived a fate that met many of its contemporaries, which were often dismantled or reshaped into cellos in later centuries.

The instrument's journey to Nice was marked by the dedication of Antoine Gautier. A passionate collector and amateur musician from Nice, Gautier bequeathed his esteemed collection to the city in his 1901 will. This significant contribution saw the viola da gamba transitioning from various municipal holdings to its permanent residence in the museum during the 2000s. Here, it is maintained in a playable condition, enriching the Palais's vibrant musical environment.

The uniqueness of Turner's creation is further underscored by its historical context. Made during the English Commonwealth period, a time when chamber music was gaining popularity, the six-string configuration met the era's demand for intimate musical performances. The palace hosts concerts where, in the delicately frescoed salon, the viola da gamba's rich tones echo the cultural grandeur of its past. The Palais Lascaris, with treasures such as this, not only preserves the music of previous centuries but also poses questions about the future innovations brought by Italian craftsmen to the evolution of bass instruments.

Orientation: As you stand before the elegant Sacqueboute ténor by Anton Schnitzer, note its place within the musical tapestry of the Palais Lascaris. This tenor sackbut is nestled in a room filled with instruments that span centuries, offering a glimpse into the evolution of music.

This extraordinary instrument was crafted in 1581 by Anton Schnitzer, an esteemed brass instrument maker from Nuremberg known for his meticulous craftsmanship. Schnitzer specialized in ceremonial brass for the Bavarian court, producing this instrument with a distinctive U-shaped slide—an innovative feature of early trombones, marking its evolution in musical history. It bears Schnitzer's mark with the engraved inscription "MACHT ANTONI SCHNITZER A[NNO] MDLXXXI" on the bell garland, an authentic signature that elevates its historical value.

For years, this sackbut was cherished at the Conservatoire National de Région de Nice. In 2001, a pivotal shift occurred when it found a new home at the Palais Lascaris, enhancing its historical context amid opulent surroundings. The eminent curator, Michel Foussard, had a hand in this transition. Foussard's efforts in relocating the instrument were instrumental in enriching the museum's collection, allowing visitors to appreciate the sackbut's rich history alongside other significant instruments like the violes gambe by William Turner that you've already seen.

With its original brass mouthpiece intact, this sackbut stands as the world's oldest preserved in original condition, an embodiment of Renaissance musical innovation. The inclusion of this rare piece highlights the Palais's mission to preserve musical heritage. As you ponder its journey, consider how it weaves together technological advancements and artistic endeavors—an intricate dance between past and present, resonating through time.

Orientation: You are about to explore the Palais Lascaris in Nice, home to a collection of exquisite musical instruments from different eras. These instruments, spanning centuries and continents, showcase the evolution and adaptation of musical craftsmanship over time. The Palais Lascaris, transformed into a music museum in 2011, houses these remarkable pieces that reflect the rich history and cultural heritage of their respective origins, now preserved for all to appreciate. At this work, you'll see the Violes gambe by William Turner (Londres, 1652), which defied the fate of many of its contemporaries. This work features the Sacqueboute ténor by Anton Schnitzer (Nuremberg, 1581), showcasing Schnitzer's meticulous skill with its U-shaped slide and parallel sliding tubes. Your first stop is Harpe by Naderman (Paris, 1780). As you stand before the Harpe by Naderman (Paris, 1780) in the ornate halls of the Palais Lascaris, notice the intricate painted floral and vegetal motifs on its soundboard, accentuated by the rich history of its journey from obscurity to display.

In 1942, the city of Nice purchased the Palais Lascaris with the intention of transforming it into a museum. This decision set in motion a series of restorations that began in 1962, reshaping the palace from a former aristocratic residence into a museum of popular art and musical instruments. As a result of this transformation, the Harpe by Naderman, discovered in the attic of the Château de Busset and purchased by the city of Nice in 2007, found its home at the Palais Lascaris, where it was first presented to the public during the European Night of Museums in May 2008. Jean-Henri Naderman, a prominent harp maker in Paris, crafted this particular harp in 1780. The harp features a single-action hook mechanism controlled by pedals, an innovation of its time that allowed harpists to modulate pitch mid-performance. This particular mechanism became a vital component that enhanced the complexity of compositions that could be played on the harp. François Joseph Naderman, Jean-Henri's son, continued the family legacy by establishing the harp studio at the Paris Conservatory in 1825, long after the creation of this harp. This studio became a focal point for harp education and innovation, nurturing generations of musicians who would carry forward the rich heritage encapsulated by Jean-Henri Naderman's craftsmanship. Through these family contributions to harp-making and music education, the Naderman name carved out a significant place in the history of Western music. As you take in the elegant artistry of this harp, consider how its crafted beauty and innovative design reflect not only the talents of its maker but also the evolving landscape of music in eighteenth-century France.
